match.reason: Neither bank point teaches how sample means vary from sample to sample or that larger samples vary less; one covers sampling methods and the other covers basic probability.

note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Remember, wording: The remember line drops the card's hedges. The card says means 'usually differ' and larger samples 'tend to' vary less, but the remember line states flatly that means change and larger samples change less. Students could read this as always true.

rejected.title: Sample means vary
card: A sample is a group taken from a larger population. Its mean is found by adding the values and dividing by the number of values.
Different samples contain different values, so their means usually differ, even when each sample is taken and worked out correctly. This is called sample variation.
Example: two samples of 3 students have heights 160, 170, 180 and 165, 175, 185. The means are 510 ÷ 3 = 170 and 525 ÷ 3 = 175.
Larger samples tend to have means that vary less from sample to sample. A single extreme value has less pull on a big sample.
rejected.remember: Sample means change from sample to sample, and larger samples change less.

a.q: Two correctly chosen random samples of 10 from the same population have different means. What does this show?
opts: Sample means vary from one sample to the next
One of the two samples was chosen wrongly
The population mean changed between samples
One of the means was calculated incorrectly
a.why: Each sample holds different values, so their means usually differ even when nothing has gone wrong. A difference does not mean a sample was chosen badly or a mean was worked out wrongly, and the population itself stays the same.
a.clue: Do two samples usually contain the same values?

b.q: Sam takes many samples of 5 from a school's students, and Lee takes many samples of 50. Whose sample means will vary less?
opts: Lee's, because the samples are larger
Sam's, because the samples are smaller
Both the same, because the school is the same
Sam's, because there are fewer values to add
b.why: A larger sample is less affected by any one extreme value, so Lee's means tend to stay closer together. Taking samples from the same school does not make the variation equal, because sample size still matters.
b.clue: Think about how much one extreme value matters in a big sample.

a.q: Two samples of the same size are taken from one population. What should we expect about their means?
opts: They will usually differ a little
They will always be identical
They will always equal the population mean
They will differ more if the samples are larger
a.why: Each sample holds different values, so the means usually differ. They are not always equal to the population mean. Larger samples vary less, not more.
a.clue: Different values go into each sample.

b.q: Sam takes many samples of 5 from a school's students, and Lee takes many samples of 50. Whose sample means will vary less?
opts: Lee's, because the samples are larger
Sam's, because the samples are smaller
Both the same, because the school is the same
Sam's, because there are fewer values to add
b.why: A larger sample is less affected by any one extreme value, so Lee's means stay closer together. The population being the same does not make the variation equal.
b.clue: Think about how much one extreme value matters in a big sample.

a.best: They will usually differ a little

b.best: Lee's, because the samples are larger

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a hedge ('usually'). The two 'always' options are easy to rule out on wording alone, so a student can pick the answer without knowing the idea.
'Differ a little' is vague. How much two sample means differ depends on sample size and the population's spread, and the card never says the difference is small.

The card defines a sample as a 'small group'. A sample need not be small, and calling it small clashes with the card's own point about larger samples. 'A group taken from a larger population' would be more accurate.

check.summary: The facts and intended answers are correct. Question a's right option stands out as the only hedged one, its 'a little' is vague, and the card wrongly says a sample is a 'small' group.
